meta.title: Who really said "For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. Feynman wrote it as the last line of Appendix F to the 1986 Rogers Commission Challenger report. NASA's text prints 'nature', not 'Nature'.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Feynman — the closing sentence of his personal Appendix F to the 1986 Challenger report, an appendix he had to fight to get published.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1918–1988 · American theoretical physicist · Nobel laureate · Rogers Commission member
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and unusually easy to prove. It is the closing sentence of Appendix F: Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle, Feynman’s personal addendum to the Presidential Commission’s report on the Challenger accident, published June 1986 — and NASA still hosts the full text ↗, where the line appears verbatim.
answer.confidenceText: Confirmed word-for-word against the U.S. government’s own published text of Appendix F.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, Vol. 2 — Appendix F: Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle
The closing sentence, ending the “Conclusions” section

source.excerpt:
NASA owes it to the citizens from whom it asks support to be frank, honest, and informative, so that these citizens can make the wisest decisions for the use of their limited resources.

For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.
trail: Fetched NASA’s official text of Appendix F ↗ and confirmed the document ends with this exact sentence, byline “by R. P. Feynman.”
Corroborated the citation against the sourced entry at WIST ↗, which places the line in Appendix F and dates it June 1986.
Dated the report from NASA’s own catalogue record, which gives 6 June 1986 ↗; President Reagan’s remarks on receiving the final report ↗ are dated 9 June 1986.

Ruled out a look-alike source: Caltech’s Engineering & Science print of Feynman’s Challenger talk (Fall 1987, edited by Ralph Leighton) is a different text and does not contain this sentence, so it is not cited here.
source.excerptNote: The final two sentences of Appendix F, transcribed from NASA’s published text. Note the lowercase “nature.”

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in the report of a U.S. federal commission, and works of the United States Government are not subject to copyright. NASA’s own catalogue record for the Commission’s report carries the statement “Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted” ↗, and NASA publishes the complete text free of charge. One caveat: Feynman’s 1988 book “What Do You Care What Other People Think?” reprints the appendix and that book is in copyright as a book — quote from the government text, not the trade edition.

author.name: Richard Feynman
author.heading: Richard P. Feynman
author.metaLine: 1918–1988 · American theoretical physicist · Rogers Commission member
author.bio: Feynman was one of the twentieth century’s great theoretical physicists — a Nobel laureate for his work on quantum electrodynamics, and a famously plain-spoken teacher who distrusted jargon and authority in roughly equal measure. In 1986 he was appointed to the Presidential Commission investigating the loss of the Space Shuttle Challenger, where he became the investigation’s most visible sceptic. His Appendix F was a personal dissent, not a committee product, and it survives as the best-known thing the Commission published.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong paperwork
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous-name quotes that survives scrutiny intact — Feynman really wrote it. What travels badly is everything around it: the spelling, the document it came from, and who is supposed to have signed off on it.

items.why: The capitalised form is extremely common — Wikiquote’s Technology page uses it ↗ even though its Richard Feynman page does not. NASA’s published text of Appendix F ↗ prints a lowercase “nature.”

It was not the Commission’s conclusion. It was Feynman’s personal appendix, which appeared only because he threatened to remove his name from the report ↗; his colleagues were alarmed by the dissent and included it after much petitioning.

items.who: A remark from the televised hearings
items.why: Even careful commentators cite it loosely — Edward Tufte’s notebook entry ↗ gives only “his report on the shuttle Challenger accident in 1986” and prints the capitalised form. The line is the final written sentence of a document, not something said at a hearing or during the famous ice-water demonstration.

“What Do You Care What Other People Think?” does include the appendix ↗, so citations to it are not wrong — but the first publication was the government report of June 1986, and that is the edition to cite.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Feynman, and genuinely his own words: the last sentence of Appendix F: Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle, in the Presidential Commission’s report of June 1986, published in full by NASA ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Feynman joined the Challenger commission as an outsider and stayed one. He concluded that NASA management had talked itself into failure odds wildly better than its own engineers believed — a finding that sat badly in a consensus report, and one that very nearly never saw print. He threatened to remove his name from the report ↗ unless his observations were included; they ran as Appendix F only after much petitioning by his fellow commissioners.

That backstory is what gives the last sentence its bite. It is not a summary of the Commission’s findings — it is the dissenter’s parting shot, written by the one member who refused to let the document close on a diplomatic note. Feynman put it at the very end of his appendix, after a paragraph arguing that NASA owed the public frankness about what the Shuttle could and could not do.
detailsBody: The sentence circulates in two forms: with a lowercase “nature” and with a capitalised “Nature.” NASA’s published text of Appendix F uses the lowercase form, and so do Wikipedia’s article on the report and the sourced entry at WIST ↗. The capitalised variant is common enough that Wikiquote carries both spellings on different pages.

Feynman later reprinted the appendix in his 1988 book “What Do You Care What Other People Think?”, which is why some citations point there. That reprint is real, but it is not where the sentence first appeared.
